Present Perfect and Simple Past
Sometimes it can be difficult to know when to use the Present Perfect Tense and when to use the Simple Past Tense, since both of them are used to talk about actions that began in the past.
You use the Present Perfect to:

1. Talk about recent events, with no definite time
For example:
We have just bought a new car.

1. Talk about events that happened at some unknown or unmentioned time in the past
For example:
I have been to Cuba three times.

1. Talk about past events that have a connection to the present
For example:
I don't want to see that movie. I've already seen it.

1. Talk about things which began in the past and are still true
For example:
I have lived here for ten years.

1. Talk about a habitual action that has been occurring frequently up to the present
For example:
I have been working out recently.
You use the Simple Past to:

1. Talk about events that occurred at a specific time in the past
For example:
I bought a car last week.

1. Talk about things that started and ended in the past.
For example:

I lived there for ten years.

Relative Clauses: What and Whatever
You can begin a clause with what or whatever. These are known as noun clauses and they can replace a noun or a noun phrase in a sentence.
What replaces a thing or the things.
In a sentence like “I couldn't believe the news,” the news is a noun phrase. A what clause can be inserted into that part of a sentence.
For example:
I couldn't believe what Mike told me yesterday.
You can also use a relative what clause at the beginning of a sentence.
For example:
What you should do is talk to your lawyer.
Whatever can be used in a similar way.
For example:
When you're old enough to live on your own, you can do whatever you want.
Whatever you do, don't tell the teacher.

images.text:
Have you ever seen a volcanic eruption? I clearly remember the day Mt. St. Helens erupted because what I saw was unforgettable. Since the scene took place, it has been locked in my memory. I won't forget it! I was trailer camping in Washington State with my father that week. We, like most people in the area, were there to "volcano watch".
Since the eruption had been predicted weeks in advance, everyone was waiting for the show to begin. No one realized what a dramatic show it would be!

That morning, I was making breakfast when my father was finished setting up the camera that we had always kept focused on the mountain. I remember what I heard: my father gasped so I came out to see what was happening.
What met my eyes was startling. It looked like one whole side of the mountain was gone, replaced by an enormous gray cloud that was expanding very quickly. Soon, it hid the entire mountain from view and seemed to be shooting thousands of feet in the air.
Since that day, I have not seen or felt anything to match what happened next. What we heard was a low rumble, and the ground shook slightly as we stood there, dumbfounded. After a few minutes, it dawned on us that not only was a dark cloud growing rapidly, but it was coming straight at us!

We grabbed the camera after snapping whatever we could of the eruption, dived into the car, and drove as quickly as we could away from the volcano. We could hear rocks and bits of hard ash bouncing against the top of the car, but we made it out of the area safely. That eruption was magnificent, and I have not experienced anything like it since . My father said that he too was both frightened and amazed. We have made a promise to look at the pictures we took once a year. We always remember that experience!
